title: Definition 2.1 --- Set
Definition 2.2 --- Three Ways to Describe a Set
content:
\textbf{1. Roster (Enumeration) Method:} List all elements explicitly inside braces.
\[
    A = \{1,\, 2,\, 3,\, 4,\, 5\}
\]

\textbf{2. Set-Builder (Predicate) Notation:} Describe elements by a property $P(x)$.
\[
    A = \{x \mid P(x)\} \quad \text{or} \quad A = \{x : P(x)\}
\]
Read: ``the set of all $x$ such that $P(x)$ is true.''

\textbf{3. Verbal Description:} Describe in plain words, e.g.\
``the set of all even positive integers less than 10.''

\vspace{0.4cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{\faInfoCircle\ Standard Number Sets:}}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{|c|l|l|}
\hline
\rowcolor{primaryblue!20}
\textbf{Symbol} & \textbf{Name} & \textbf{Elements} \\
\hline
$\mathbb{N}$ & Natural numbers & $\{0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$ \\
\hline
$\mathbb{Z}$ & Integers & $\{\ldots, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, \ldots\}$ \\
\hline
$\mathbb{Z}^+$ & Positive integers & $\{1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$ \\
\hline
$\mathbb{Q}$ & Rational numbers & $\{p/q \mid p,q \in \mathbb{Z},\, q \neq 0\}$ \\
\hline
$\mathbb{R}$ & Real numbers & All points on the number line \\
\hline
$\mathbb{C}$ & Complex numbers & $\{a + bi \mid a,b \in \mathbb{R}\}$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Definition 2.4 --- Subset and Proper Subset
content:
Set $A$ is a \textbf{subset} of set $B$, written $A \subseteq B$, if every element
of $A$ is also an element of $B$:
\[
    A \subseteq B \iff \forall x\,(x \in A \rightarrow x \in B)
\]

Set $A$ is a \textbf{proper subset} of $B$, written $A \subset B$ (or $A \subsetneq B$),
if $A \subseteq B$ \textbf{and} $A \neq B$ (i.e., $B$ has at least one element not in $A$).

\vspace{0.4cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{\faInfoCircle\ Key Properties:}}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
    \item $\emptyset \subseteq A$ for \textbf{every} set $A$
          (the empty set is a subset of every set).
    \item $A \subseteq A$ for every set $A$ (every set is a subset of itself).
    \item $A = B \iff (A \subseteq B) \land (B \subseteq A)$
    \item If $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq C$, then $A \subseteq C$ (transitivity).
    \item $A \not\subseteq B$ means $\exists x\,(x \in A \land x \notin B)$.
\end{itemize}

\vspace{0.5cm}

title: Example 2: Identifying Subsets
content:
Let $A = \{1, 2\}$, $B = \{1, 2, 3\}$, $C = \{2, 3, 4\}$, $D = \{1, 2\}$.

Determine which of the following are true:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), leftmargin=2em]
    \item $A \subseteq B$
    \item $B \subseteq A$
    \item $A \subset D$
    \item $A = D$
    \item $\emptyset \subseteq A$
    \item $A \subseteq C$
\end{enumerate}

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{Solution:}}

\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{|c|l|c|}
\hline
\rowcolor{primaryblue!20}
\textbf{Statement} & \textbf{Reasoning} & \textbf{True/False} \\
\hline
$A \subseteq B$ & $1 \in B$ and $2 \in B$, so every element of $A$ is in $B$ &
\textcolor{darkgreen}{\checkmark\ True} \\
\hline
$B \subseteq A$ & $3 \in B$ but $3 \notin A$, so $B \not\subseteq A$ &
\textcolor{red}{$\times$\ False} \\
\hline
$A \subset D$ & $A \subseteq D$ but $A = D$ (not proper) &
\textcolor{red}{$\times$\ False} \\
\hline
$A = D$ & Both contain exactly $\{1,2\}$ &
\textcolor{darkgreen}{\checkmark\ True} \\
\hline
$\emptyset \subseteq A$ & Empty set is subset of every set &
\textcolor{darkgreen}{\checkmark\ True} \\
\hline
$A \subseteq C$ & $1 \in A$ but $1 \notin C$ &
\textcolor{red}{$\times$\ False} \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{0.5cm}

title: Definition 2.5 --- Cardinality
Definition 2.6 --- Power Set
Theorem 2.1 --- Cardinality of the Power Set
content:
If $A$ is a finite set with $|A| = n$, then:
\[
    |\mathcal{P}(A)| = 2^n
\]
In particular, $|\mathcal{P}(\emptyset)| = 2^0 = 1$,
since $\mathcal{P}(\emptyset) = \{\emptyset\}$.

Definition 2.11 --- Set Difference and Symmetric Difference
content:
The \textbf{set difference} (or \textit{relative complement}) of $B$ from $A$,
written $A - B$ or $A \setminus B$, is the set of elements in $A$ but \textbf{not} in $B$:
\[
    A - B = \{x \mid x \in A \land x \notin B\} = A \cap \overline{B}
\]

\vspace{0.3cm}
The \textbf{symmetric difference} of $A$ and $B$, written $A \oplus B$
(or $A \triangle B$), is the set of elements in \textbf{exactly one} of $A$ or $B$:
\[
    A \oplus B = (A - B) \cup (B - A) = (A \cup B) - (A \cap B)
\]

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textcolor{accentorange}{\textbf{Note:}} $A \oplus B$ in set theory corresponds to
$p \oplus q$ (exclusive or) in propositional logic.
Past Paper 2023 Q1(x) asks to draw the Venn diagram for symmetric difference.

Example 3: Set-Builder Proof of De Morgan --- Past Paper 2022 Q6(a)
content:
Use set-builder notation and logical equivalences to establish:
\[
    (A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'
\]

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{Solution:}}

\vspace{0.3cm}
We prove this by showing membership equivalence:

\begin{align*}
    x \in (A \cap B)'
    &\iff x \notin A \cap B \\
    &\iff \neg(x \in A \land x \in B) \\
    &\iff (\neg\, x \in A) \lor (\neg\, x \in B)
        &&\text{De Morgan's Law for logic} \\
    &\iff (x \notin A) \lor (x \notin B) \\
    &\iff x \in A' \lor x \in B' \\
    &\iff x \in A' \cup B'
\end{align*}

\vspace{0.2cm}
Since $x \in (A \cap B)'$ if and only if $x \in A' \cup B'$:
\[
    \boxed{(A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'} \qed
\]

Definition 2.13 --- Binary Relation
content:
A \textbf{binary relation} $R$ from set $A$ to set $B$ is a subset of the
Cartesian product $A \times B$:
\[
    R \subseteq A \times B
\]
We write $a\, R\, b$ or $(a,b) \in R$ to mean ``$a$ is related to $b$ by $R$.''

\vspace{0.4cm}
When $A = B$, we say $R$ is a \textbf{relation on $A$}, meaning $R \subseteq A \times A$.

\vspace{0.4cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{\faInfoCircle\ Key Points:}}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
    \item A relation is simply a \textbf{set of ordered pairs}.
    \item A relation on $A$ with $|A| = n$ is a subset of $A \times A$,
          which has $n^2$ elements. So there are $2^{n^2}$ possible relations on $A$.
    \item Relations can be represented as: a \textbf{set of ordered pairs},
          a \textbf{directed graph} (digraph), or a \textbf{matrix}.
\end{itemize}

\vspace{0.5cm}

title: Definition 2.14 --- Matrix Representation of a Relation
content:
The \textbf{relation matrix} (or \textit{Boolean matrix}) $M_R$ of a relation
$R$ on $A = \{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n\}$ is an $n \times n$ matrix where:
\[
    M_R[i][j] =
    \begin{cases}
        1 & \text{if } (a_i,\, a_j) \in R \\
        0 & \text{if } (a_i,\, a_j) \notin R
    \end{cases}
\]

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textbf{Digraph representation:} Draw a vertex for each element of $A$.
Draw a directed edge (arrow) from $a_i$ to $a_j$ whenever $(a_i, a_j) \in R$.
A \textbf{loop} at vertex $a_i$ represents the pair $(a_i, a_i) \in R$.

\vspace{0.5cm}

Definition 2.17 --- Antisymmetric Relation
content:
A relation $R$ on set $A$ is \textbf{antisymmetric} if whenever both
$(a,b) \in R$ and $(b,a) \in R$, then $a = b$:
\[
    R \text{ is antisymmetric} \iff \forall a,b \in A,\;
    [(a,b) \in R \land (b,a) \in R \rightarrow a = b]
\]

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{\faInfoCircle\ Key Points:}}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
    \item Equivalently: if $a \neq b$ and $(a,b) \in R$, then $(b,a) \notin R$.
    \item \textbf{Antisymmetric $\neq$ not symmetric.} A relation can be both
          symmetric and antisymmetric (e.g.\ the equality relation on a single element).
    \item In the \textbf{matrix}: for $i \neq j$, $M[i][j]$ and $M[j][i]$
          cannot \textit{both} be 1.
    \item Example: ``$\leq$'' on integers is antisymmetric
          ($a \leq b$ and $b \leq a$ implies $a = b$).
\end{itemize}

\vspace{0.5cm}

title: Definition 2.18 --- Transitive Relation
content:
A relation $R$ on set $A$ is \textbf{transitive} if whenever $(a,b) \in R$
and $(b,c) \in R$, then $(a,c) \in R$:
\[
    R \text{ is transitive} \iff \forall a,b,c \in A,\;
    [(a,b) \in R \land (b,c) \in R \rightarrow (a,c) \in R]
\]

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{\faInfoCircle\ Recognition Tips:}}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
    \item In the \textbf{digraph}: if there is a path $a \to b \to c$,
          there must also be a direct edge $a \to c$.
    \item To \textbf{disprove}: find $a,b,c$ with $(a,b),(b,c) \in R$
          but $(a,c) \notin R$.
    \item \textbf{Careful:} check \textit{all} pairs systematically ---
          one missed pair makes it non-transitive.
\end{itemize}

Definition 2.22 --- Partition
content:
A \textbf{partition} of a set $A$ is a collection of non-empty, mutually disjoint
subsets $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_k$ (called \textbf{cells} or \textbf{blocks}) whose
union is $A$:
\[
    A = A_1 \cup A_2 \cup \cdots \cup A_k
    \quad \text{where} \quad
    A_i \neq \emptyset
    \quad \text{and} \quad
    A_i \cap A_j = \emptyset \text{ for } i \neq j
\]

\vspace{0.4cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{\faInfoCircle\ Key Points:}}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
    \item Every partition of $A$ defines an equivalence relation on $A$:
          $a \sim b$ iff $a$ and $b$ are in the \textbf{same cell}.
    \item Conversely, every equivalence relation on $A$ induces a partition of $A$
          (the cells are the equivalence classes).
    \item This is the \textbf{Fundamental Theorem of Equivalence Relations}
          (Theorem~2.6 below).
    \item The set of all equivalence classes is called the \textbf{quotient set},
          written $A / R$.
\end{itemize}

\vspace{0.5cm}

title: Theorem 2.6 --- Fundamental Theorem of Equivalence Relations
content:
Let $R$ be an equivalence relation on a non-empty set $A$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), leftmargin=2em]
    \item The equivalence classes of $R$ form a \textbf{partition} of $A$.
    \item Conversely, given any partition $\{A_1, A_2, \ldots\}$ of $A$,
          the relation defined by $a \sim b \iff a$ and $b$ are in the same cell
          is an equivalence relation on $A$.
\end{enumerate}
This establishes a \textbf{one-to-one correspondence} between equivalence relations
on $A$ and partitions of $A$.

{primaryblue}{{\ Exam Preparation Tips for Chapter
content:
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{\faLightbulb\ Exam Preparation Tips for Chapter 2}}

\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
    \item \textbf{Q1--Q3} cover sets and power sets --- always in objective part
          (2 marks each).
    \item \textbf{Q4--Q8} cover set operations --- De Morgan proofs appear almost
          every year as a 12-mark subjective question.
    \item \textbf{Q9--Q11} are the most heavily tested topic in this course ---
          relations and their properties appear as full subjective questions in
          2020, 2021, 2022, and 2024.
    \item \textbf{Q12--Q13} on equivalence relations are typically worth 12 marks
          when they appear. Always verify all three properties with clear steps.
    \item \textbf{Q14--Q20} on partial orders and Hasse diagrams are growing in
          frequency --- master the construction rules and special element definitions.
\end{itemize}
